title: Halbach Array Tour
description: Guided walkthrough of a rotating-magnetisation array: point-dipole superposition, the rotation step, why the field piles up on one side, and how it pairs with the Hall bench.

steps.title: Magnets arranged to push the field one way
steps.body: A row of identical magnets gives the same field on both faces. Rotate each magnet's orientation a fixed step from its neighbour and the field adds up on one side and thins out on the other. That is a Halbach array, and this bench lets you build one from 4 to 24 segments and see the field it makes.

steps.title: Step 1 — segments are point dipoles
steps.body: The drive slider sets the segment count N (4 at the bottom, 24 at the top). Each segment is one point dipole, coloured by its orientation, and the field anywhere is the sum of every dipole's field. The λ in the readout is the spacing between segments, and the array is a ring by default; add ?halbachLinear=1 to the URL for a straight row.

steps.title: Step 2 — the rotation step
steps.body: The same slider also sweeps the magnetisation step between neighbours from 0.65× to 1.35× the ideal 360°/N. At half drive it is exactly the ideal step, and in the ring each magnet's orientation turns twice for every lap round the circle — the Halbach pattern. The θ readout is the step actually in use.

steps.title: Step 3 — one side strong, one side weak
steps.body: Look straight down on the |B| slice and the field lines. In this model the ring packs its field inside the bore, where it reads several times the value outside; the straight row puts roughly three to six times more field on one face than on the other. That asymmetry is the point of the pattern: the same magnet material, steered onto the side you want. Across the slider's whole sweep the asymmetry never disappears; the step changes how strong each side is, not whether there is a weak one.

steps.title: Step 4 — reading |B| and F honestly
steps.body: The |B| readout is the largest value found on a coarse grid of sample points near the array. Because each magnet is a point dipole, that maximum jumps when a sample point lands close to one — use it to compare settings, not as a surface-field specification. F is a force proxy: the gradient of m·B on a small test dipole held above the array.

steps.title: Step 5 — a field source for the Hall bench
steps.body: Switch on Lab field coupling (it is off by default) and this array's peak |B| becomes the Hall strip's field, clamped to that bench's range. The Hall voltage then follows the number you are reading here. It is one simulated estimate feeding another simulated plant — it teaches the dependence, but nothing in the chain is a measurement.

steps.title: What this model is not
steps.body: A superposition of idealised point dipoles. There is no finite magnet size or shape, no demagnetisation, no permeable backing, no temperature and no manufacturing tolerance, and it has no C++ plant — the field is computed in JavaScript. It is a picture of the pattern, not a magnet design tool: do not read a build specification off it.
